sections.label: SMS Sender ID Registry questions
sections.summary: Questions ask why the anti-SMS spoofing registry shut, whether agencies had time, and how the new SSIR is superior and aligned internationally.

sentences.speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng
sentences.text: asked the Minister for Communications and Information (a) why was the anti-SMS spoofing registry shut just about over a month after Government agencies announced their intent to join the registry; (b) whether adequate time was given for the agencies to assess the new decision; (c) what are the ways by which the full-fledged Singapore SMS Sender ID Registry will be superior; (d) how will it put us in line with international practices; and (e) what is the timeline for banks, Government agencies and interested organisations to be fully onboarded.

sentences.speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Communications and Information)
sentences.text: It replaced the SMS SenderID Registry pilot, which was started by IMDA and MAS in August 2021 and that pilot was done in collaboration with the UK Mobile Ecosystem Forum (MEF).

sentences.speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Communications and Information)
sentences.text: Under the previous MEF model, spoofed SMSes that use a registered Sender ID will still be received by consumers until the Sender ID owner confirms that the spoofed SMSes are not legitimate and should be blocked.

sentences.speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Communications and Information)
sentences.text: The new SSIR takes a more proactive approach.

sentences.speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Communications and Information)
sentences.text: It can block spoofed SMSes upfront and provide a greater control over anti-spoof measures that better protect Singaporeans.

sections.label: Singapore national SMS Sender ID Registry
sections.summary: Singapore is among the first countries with a national SMS Sender ID Registry, and 25 organisations joined SSIR as of 30 March 2022.

sentences.speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Communications and Information)
sentences.text: Internationally, Singapore is one of the first few countries to have implemented a national SMS Sender ID Registry to better prevent spoofed SMSes.

sentences.speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Communications and Information)
sentences.text: As of 30 March 2022, 25 organisations, including banks and Government agencies, have joined SSIR.

sections.label: SSIR fees and Sender IDs
sections.summary: Organisations pay a one-time $500 set-up fee and $1,000 per 10 Sender IDs, with over 1,000 protected Sender IDs as of 30 March.

sentences.speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
sentences.text: Specifically, organisations would pay a one-time set-up fee of $500 and $1,000 for every 10 Sender IDs.

sentences.speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
sentences.text: Having said that, so far, as of 30 March, there are more than 1,000 protected SMS Sender IDs in the registry already.

sentences.speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
sentences.text: So, IMDA will monitor the landscape to study if the registration of SMS Sender IDs should be mandatory or if there should be another framework in place.
